prompt: PowerInfo, in this folder, is a small .NET console app. Add a `GetBatteryPercent()` method to the `PowerStatus` class in `Battery.cs` that returns the current battery charge as a percentage. Use the Windows Runtime APIs that ship with Windows, not P/Invoke or WMI. This machine has no battery, so you can't check the value by running it, but the project must still build.

reference.approach: Target a Windows 10 SDK framework (net10.0-windows10.0.19041.0) so the WinRT projection is referenced. In GetBatteryPercent, call Windows.Devices.Power.Battery.AggregateBattery.GetReport() and return RemainingCapacityInMilliwattHours * 100 / FullChargeCapacityInMilliwattHours, or null when either value is missing. BatteryReport has no percentage property.

checks: builds (required, guard): `dotnet build` of PowerInfo.csproj succeeds when the checker runs it. The fixture already builds, so this only guards against breaking it
method-callable (required): a probe file that calls `PowerInfo.PowerStatus.GetBatteryPercent()` with no arguments and uses its return value compiles
battery-api (required): Battery.cs gets a report from Windows.Devices.Power.Battery (AggregateBattery or FromIdAsync, then GetReport())
percent-from-capacity (required): Battery.cs reads RemainingCapacityInMilliwattHours and FullChargeCapacityInMilliwattHours and divides
no-stand-ins (required, guard): no workspace source declares its own Battery or BatteryReport type, or members with the battery API's names
windows-sdk-tfm: the project evaluates to a net*-windows10.* target framework
whyGoodTest: The most common reason to look up an API: the developer knows the goal (battery percentage), not the type name. Agents without a lookup tend to invent a plausible member such as a percentage property, which BatteryReport doesn't have; the checker's build catches an invented member, so the test is fair without judging style. It needs no battery: the checker only builds and reads the code, and the probe proves the method exists without running it.
